name: Train Length, Pole Crossings, and Speed Units
description: Build the core train model: crossing a point means the whole train moves one train-length, with quick km/hr ↔ m/s conversion.
script_scope: Teach that a train has cleared a pole, signal, tree, or standing person only when its rear has passed the point, so the distance travelled equals the train's own length. Cover km/hr to m/s using ×5/18 and m/s to km/hr using ×18/5, then use distance = speed × time to find crossing time, train length, or speed. Include same-speed length scaling, minute/second conversion, and the chapter's equally spaced pillar-count idea where the starting pillar makes the count one more than the number of gaps. Keep the mental model visual: front enters, rear clears, one train-length has moved.

name: Platforms, Bridges, and Tunnels
description: Extend the crossing model to long stationary objects by adding the train length to the object length.
script_scope: Teach that to completely cross a platform, bridge, or tunnel, the train's front must travel the train length plus the object's length. Use this to find crossing time, train length, platform/bridge/tunnel length, and speed. Cover objects that are a multiple of the train length, and develop the extra-time shortcut: compared with crossing a pole, the additional time is exactly the time needed to cover the platform or bridge length. Include two-platform comparisons where the difference in crossing times corresponds to the difference in platform lengths.

name: Finding Train Length and Speed from Multiple Crossing Times
description: Use two observations of the same train to eliminate unknowns and recover its speed, length, or another object's length.
script_scope: Teach inference from repeated crossings: pole time plus platform time, two platform lengths with two times, a pole plus a stationary train, and equal-length stationary-train cases. Emphasize subtraction before algebra: the train length appears in both observations, so subtracting the distances often removes it instantly. Then recover the train length from speed × pole time. Include capstones that combine a pole, a platform, and a stationary train in one chain.

name: Trains Passing People, Runners, and Cyclists
description: Use relative speed when the object being passed is moving, subtracting for the same direction and adding for the opposite direction.
script_scope: Teach moving-person crossings with relative speed. In the same direction use train speed minus person speed; in opposite directions use the sum. Cover finding crossing time, train speed, and train length; a jogger with an initial lead; a cyclist whose cycle length slightly increases the distance; a passenger in one train observing an opposite train; and the two-walker pattern where one train overtakes walkers at different speeds in different times, allowing train speed and length to be inferred.

name: Two Trains Moving in Opposite Directions
description: Add relative speeds and add train lengths to solve head-on crossings, unknown lengths, unknown speeds, and initial-gap problems.
script_scope: Teach head-on train crossings as one closing problem: total distance to clear = sum of train lengths, relative speed = sum of speeds. Use this to find crossing time, an unknown length, or an unknown speed. Include equal-speed trains, trains initially separated by a gap, a passenger in one train timing the other, equal-length trains with known pole-crossing times, and the chapter pattern where two trains start a fixed distance apart and the same separation reappears after they cross.

name: Overtaking Trains in the Same Direction
description: Subtract train speeds and use the sum of their lengths to model one train completely overtaking another.
script_scope: Teach overtaking as relative motion: the faster train must gain a distance equal to both train lengths, so use speed difference and sum of lengths. Cover time to overtake, unknown faster/slower speed, equal-length trains, trains starting together, an explicit head start, speed ratios obtained from same-direction versus opposite-direction crossing times, and the two-walker inference pattern as a transfer exercise.

name: Train Meetings Between Stations and Timetables
description: Solve when and where trains meet, including delayed starts, distance differences at the meeting point, and after-meeting travel times.
script_scope: Teach station-to-station meeting problems using closing speed after accounting for any head start. Cover simultaneous starts, delayed starts, finding route length from the difference in distances travelled at meeting, and meeting times from full-route travel times. Teach the chapter's after-meeting relation: when two trains start simultaneously from opposite ends, meet, then take a and b hours to reach the far ends, their speed ratio is sqrt(b):sqrt(a). Use it to recover speeds and route length. Finish with timetable capstones that convert a start delay into distance already covered before closing begins.

name: Advanced Mixed Train Puzzles and Shortcuts
description: Combine crossing models to solve ratio, scaling, bogie, platform, and multi-condition train puzzles efficiently.
script_scope: Teach higher-transfer patterns from the objective exercise: crossing-time ratios at the same speed, platform length as a multiple of train length, equal-length trains whose pole times predict their mutual crossing time, bogie-count changes that scale train length and crossing time, a train crossing another train and then a platform, and chained problems where a pole/platform observation determines train A before it meets train B. Encourage learners to cancel common train lengths or common speeds before calculating and to ask what distance the front must gain for the event to be complete.

name: Data Sufficiency for Train Problems
description: Decide whether the given statements determine the requested train speed, length, crossing time, or arrival time without doing unnecessary calculation.
script_scope: Teach data sufficiency using the chapter's dedicated exercise. Start by listing the quantities a train formula needs, then test Statement I alone, Statement II alone, and combinations. Cover pole crossings, platforms, stationary trains, moving trains, direction ambiguity, three-statement questions where any two suffice, and redundancy questions. The learner's goal is not to solve every number fully; it is to know whether one unique answer is forced. Use fresh train scenarios parallel to the book's DS patterns.
